title: Which engine computer (ECU) the swap runs on
ask: Which engine computer should the LS swap be designed around?
why: The engine computer sets how the new engine leg is pinned at the dash (K5), how the engine talks to the rest of the car on CAN (it has to send its own messages at 0x500 and up so the gauges and the power unit read rpm, coolant and road speed), what laptop software tunes it, and whether the hunt for the engine can stay open to both engine generations in D-393's list (the L33, LM4 and LM7 use the older 24-tooth crank signal, the LH6 and LC9 the newer 58-tooth). It is the most expensive electrical part of the swap. Prices below are from memory and were not checked this run; they are confirmed before anything is bought (BR06). The candidates are in table options, OP60 to OP63.
options:
(a) ECUMaster EMU PRO, about $1,800-2,400 (confirm): the same maker and the same laptop software family as the power unit (PMU), sends any CAN message we define, reads either crank signal so any engine on the list works, built to take our own harness through the dash post. Forecloses nothing; the dearest option but one.
(b) Holley Terminator X Max with drive-by-wire, about $1,700-2,100 (confirm): popular, comes with a ready-made engine harness and a wideband sensor. The ready-made harness is built for a computer in the engine bay, so it would be cut and re-ended at the dash post; custom CAN messages are limited (confirm). Buy the 24-tooth or 58-tooth kit to match the engine found.
(c) A factory GM engine computer matched to the engine, plus HP Tuners, about $600-1,000 all in (confirm): the cheapest and very well proven. It only speaks GM's own CAN messages, so a small translator node is needed to put rpm and coolant at 0x500 and up; it must match the engine's generation, and needs a separate wideband controller.
(d) Haltech Elite 2500, about $2,500-3,500 (confirm): top-end, fully configurable CAN and both crank signals. The most money, a second software family beside the PMU's.
recommend: (a), unless saving about $1,000 matters more than one software family and CAN without a translator - then (c)
stops: K5 (pinning the leg at the dash), the swap's ECU budget line (DS10) and the design freeze (DS11)

title: Which in-tank fuel pump the LS runs on
ask: Which in-tank fuel pump should the LS swap use at its 58 psi fuel pressure?
why: The pump decides how the FB's tank is opened for an in-tank pump, how much power the fuel system can carry later, and what the fuel pump's soft fuse on O5 is set to (D-173). The rest of the fuel system follows the LS standard and is not a choice: 58 psi returnless, with a Corvette-style filter-regulator on a single feed line. The currents are V-040's figures at 58 psi from the makers' curves. Prices were not checked this run and are confirmed before anything is bought (BR06). Whichever pump is chosen, the tank top is measured first (DS12), because nobody has looked at it for this.
options:
(a) Aeromotive Phantom 340, the candidate already named in HO12: a universal in-tank pump with its own baffle, fitted through a hole cut in the top of the existing tank. About 12.2 A, leaving O5 about half its 25 A spare. Carries a stock 5.3 easily and leaves room for a lot more power later. The tank is cut, and that cannot be undone.
(b) A 255 lph pump (Walbro/TI GSS342) on a universal in-tank hanger: about 8.9 A and cheaper. It carries a stock or mildly built 5.3 with margin, but a big power increase later (boost) would need a second pump. The tank is opened the same way.
(c) A 450 lph pump (TI F90000267/274): about 15.3 A, the least margin on O5, and 19 A at its relief valve. It is only worth it for a boosted engine.
recommend: (a), unless the engine will stay near stock power for good - then (b) is cheaper and draws about 3 A less
stops: DS05's parts list, the fuel line in the swap budget (DS10), the design freeze (DS11) and the fuel work CP06
